6.4 Solving linear systems on a computer
6.6 Computer lab: Excel, MATLAB and Python

html:
Calculus tells us how things change; computational methods tell us how to get numbers out when no neat formula exists.

This unit covers the last unit of the TU syllabus: linear programming (graphical method, simplex method up to three variables, duality) and the numerical methods that a computer actually runs: matrix inversion, Gauss elimination, Gauss-Seidel iteration, the bisection method and the Newton-Raphson method.

What this unit gives you
  • Formulating a linear programming problem (LPP) and solving two-variable problems graphically with corner points.
  • The simplex method in tableau form, slack variables, pivoting, and reading the optimum.
  • The dual of an LPP and the duality theorem.
  • Solving A X = B by matrix inversion, Gauss elimination (with back substitution) and Gauss-Seidel iteration.
  • Finding roots of f(x) = 0 by bisection and Newton-Raphson, with error control.
  • How the methods behave: special LPP cases, degeneracy and sensitivity, pivoting and ill-conditioning, convergence order, and when Newton-Raphson fails.
  • Running everything in Excel, MATLAB and Python, as the syllabus's "(Excel/Matlab)" note requires.

6.1 Linear programming problems

A linear programming problem asks us to maximise or minimise a linear objective function subject to linear constraints (inequalities) and non-negativity conditions. Typical uses: product mix, diet cost, transport, and scheduling.

Steps of formulation: (1) name the decision variables (x, y); (2) write the objective Z = c_{1} x + c_{2} y; (3) write each resource limit as an inequality; (4) add x, y \ge 0.

Worked example: formulating a product-mix problem

A computer lab assembles two products. A router kit gives a profit of Rs 3,000 and uses 1 hour of soldering and 1 hour of testing. A sensor kit gives Rs 2,000 and uses 3 hours of soldering and 1 hour of testing.

The lab has 6 soldering hours and 4 testing hours per day. Let x = routers, y = sensors (in units of Rs 1,000 profit). Maximise Z = 3 x + 2 y subject to x + 3 y \le 6 (soldering), x + y \le 4 (testing), x, y \ge 0.

Linear inequalities and the feasible region

A linear inequality in two variables, a x + b y \le c, describes a half-plane. To graph it: draw the line a x + b y = c, test the origin (0, 0) and shade the side that satisfies the inequality.

The feasible region is the intersection of all the half-planes. It is a convex polygon (or unbounded region).

The graphical (corner point) method

The key theorem: if an optimum exists, it occurs at a corner point (vertex) of the feasible region. So: (1) draw the region, (2) find every corner by solving pairs of boundary lines, (3) evaluate Z at each corner, (4) choose the largest (maximum) or smallest (minimum).

Worked example: graphical solution

Corners: O(0,0); A(4,0) from y = 0 and x + y = 4 (check x + 3 y = 4 \le 6); C(0,2) from x = 0 and x + 3 y = 6; B from x + y = 4 and x + 3 y = 6: subtract to get 2 y = 2, y = 1, x = 3. Z(O) = 0, Z(A) = 12, Z(B) = 9 + 2 = 11, Z(C) = 4.

Maximum Z = 12 at x = 4, y = 0 (4 router kits, no sensor kits; profit Rs 12,000). Soldering time used is 4 of 6 hours, so 2 hours are left over (slack).

Special cases.

No feasible region the constraints contradict each other.

Unbounded the region extends forever in the direction of improvement and the maximum does not exist.

Multiple optima the objective line is parallel to a boundary edge, so every point on that edge (and both its corners) is optimal.

Degeneracy more than two lines meet at a corner.

Formulating more problems

The hardest step in any LPP is not the arithmetic but the translation from words to inequalities.

Two further models show the usual patterns: a minimisation with \ge constraints (a diet or cost problem) and a three-variable maximisation (a product mix with three resources).

Worked example: a minimum-cost diet

A hostel mess mixes two foods. Food 1 costs Rs 20 per unit and gives 2 units of protein and 1 unit of iron. Food 2 costs Rs 30 per unit and gives 1 unit of protein and 2 units of iron.

Each student needs at least 8 units of protein and 10 units of iron per day. Find the cheapest mix.

Let x = units of Food 1 and y = units of Food 2. Minimise Z = 20 x + 30 y subject to 2 x + y \ge 8 (protein), x + 2 y \ge 10 (iron), x, y \ge 0.

The feasible region lies above both lines and is unbounded, but because the costs are positive Z cannot fall forever, so a minimum exists at a corner.

Corners: (0, 8) from x = 0 and 2 x + y = 8; (10, 0) from y = 0 and x + 2 y = 10; and the intersection of the two lines: subtract 2 \times (iron) from (protein) to get -3 y = -12, y = 4, x = 2. Z(0, 8) = 240, Z(2, 4) = 40 + 120 = 160, Z(10, 0) = 200.

Minimum cost Rs 160 at x = 2, y = 4. Both nutrient constraints are exactly met, so nothing is wasted.

Worked example: three products, three resources

A workshop makes products A, B, C with profits Rs 5, 4 and 3 (in thousands) per unit. Machine hours, labour hours and material (kg) are limited to 5, 11 and 8.

Per unit of A, B, C: machine time is 2, 3, 1; labour 4, 1, 2; material 3, 4, 2. Let x, y, z be the quantities.

Maximise Z = 5 x + 4 y + 3 z subject to 2 x + 3 y + z \le 5, \quad 4 x + y + 2 z \le 11, \quad 3 x + 4 y + 2 z \le 8, \quad x, y, z \ge 0.

This has three variables, so a drawing is impossible and we use the simplex method in 6.2, which gives x = 2, y = 0, z = 1 and Z = 13.

How to translate a word problem

Underline the quantity you control (these are the variables), the single number to maximise or minimise (objective), and every phrase like at most, at least, no more than, a minimum of (constraints). "At most" gives \le, "at least" gives \ge.

Always write the units next to each constraint, and state x, y \ge 0.

The three special cases in pictures

Not every LPP has one neat optimum. Three things can go wrong, and each has a clear graphical signature.

Special cases of an LPP

Infeasible: the constraints contradict each other, so the feasible region is empty and there is no solution.

Unbounded: the region extends to infinity in the direction in which Z improves, so the optimum does not exist (this almost always means a constraint was left out of the model).

Alternative (multiple) optima: the objective line is parallel to a boundary edge, so a whole edge is optimal. The theory of the simplex method tells us how each case appears in the tableau (6.2).

Worked example: recognising each case

(a) Maximise Z = x + y subject to x + y \le 2 and x + y \ge 4. No point can have x + y both at most 2 and at least 4: infeasible.(b) Maximise Z = x + y subject to x - y \le 2 and y - x \le 3. Along the line y = x, every point is feasible and Z = 2 x grows without limit: unbounded.(c) Maximise Z = 2 x + 2 y subject to x + y \le 4, x \le 3, y \le 3. Corners: (0,0), (3,0), (3,1), (1,3), (0,3) with Z = 0, 6, 8, 8, 6. Two adjacent corners tie at the maximum Z = 8, so every point on the edge between them, such as (2, 2), is also optimal: multiple optima.

Why only corners matter

The feasible region is convex: the segment joining any two feasible points stays inside. The objective is a linear function, so on any line segment it is largest at an end, never in the middle.

Applying this idea again and again shows that no interior point or edge point can beat the best corner. This is also why the simplex method only needs to visit corners.

6.2 The simplex method (up to three variables)

The graphical method fails beyond two variables. The simplex method moves from corner to better corner algebraically, using a table (tableau).

Standard form (maximise). Convert each \le constraint to an equation by adding a slack variable (s_{1}, s_{2} \ge 0) that measures unused resource. The objective is written Z - 3 x - 2 y = 0 so that its row holds the coefficients -3 and -2.

Algorithm.

  1. Write the initial tableau. The slack variables are the first basic variables (value = right-hand side).
  2. Entering variable: the column with the most negative entry in the objective row. If no entry is negative, stop: the solution is optimal.
  3. Leaving variable (minimum ratio test): divide each right-hand side by the positive entry of the entering column and choose the smallest ratio; that row is the pivot row.
  4. Pivot: divide the pivot row by the pivot element, then use row operations to make all other entries of the entering column zero.
  5. Repeat from step 2.
Worked example: simplex on the product-mix problem

Maximise Z = 3 x + 2 y, x + y + s_{1} = 4, x + 3 y + s_{2} = 6.

Basis x y s_1 s_2 RHS ratio
s_1 1 1 1 0 4 4 / 1 = 4
s_2 1 3 0 1 6 6 / 1 = 6
Z -3 -2 0 0 0

x enters (most negative -3); ratios 4 and 6, so row s_1 leaves; pivot element 1. Row operations: R_{2} \leftarrow R_{2} - R_{1}, R_{Z} \leftarrow R_{Z} + 3 R_{1}.

Basis x y s_1 s_2 RHS
x 1 1 1 0 4
s_2 0 2 -1 1 2
Z 0 1 3 0 12

The objective row has no negative entry, so this is optimal: x = 4, y = 0, s_{2} = 2, Z = 12, the same as the graphical answer (and the slack of 2 matches the 2 unused soldering hours).

Reading the tableau. A basic variable equals the RHS of its row; non-basic variables are zero.

In the final objective row, the entries under the slack variables (3 under s_{1}) are the shadow prices: one more testing hour would raise Z by 3 (Rs 3,000). The entry 0 under s_{2} says extra soldering time is worthless now.

For a minimisation problem, either maximise -Z, or solve the dual (6.3). For \ge constraints the big-M or two-phase method is used; the TU syllabus requires only the \le type with up to three variables.

What the simplex method does geometrically

Each tableau is one corner of the feasible region.

A pivot slides along one edge to a neighbouring corner with a better Z; the minimum-ratio test stops the slide exactly where the next constraint is reached, so the new point stays feasible.

For Z = 2 x + 3 y on the region of the product-mix problem, the path is O \to C \to B.

Simplex with three variables

The method is identical; only the tableau is wider. We solve the three-product problem formulated above: maximise Z = 5 x + 4 y + 3 z subject to 2 x + 3 y + z \le 5, 4 x + y + 2 z \le 11, 3 x + 4 y + 2 z \le 8.

Worked example: a full three-variable simplex

Initial tableau (three slack variables s_1, s_2, s_3 form the starting basis).

Basis x y z s_1 s_2 s_3 RHS ratio
s_1 2 3 1 1 0 0 5 5/2
s_2 4 1 2 0 1 0 11 11/4
s_3 3 4 2 0 0 1 8 8/3
Z -5 -4 -3 0 0 0 0

x enters (most negative, -5). Ratios 2.5,\ 2.75,\ 2.667: the smallest is 2.5, so s_1 leaves; pivot element 2. Divide row 1 by 2, then eliminate x from the other rows.

Basis x y z s_1 s_2 s_3 RHS ratio
x 1 3/2 1/2 1/2 0 0 5/2 5
s_2 0 -5 0 -2 1 0 1 none (entry 0)
s_3 0 -1/2 1/2 -3/2 0 1 1/2 1
Z 0 7/2 -1/2 5/2 0 0 25/2

Only the z column entry -1/2 is negative, so z enters. Ratios are only taken for positive entries: 5 and 1. Row s_3 leaves; pivot element \frac{1}{2}.

Basis x y z s_1 s_2 s_3 RHS
x 1 2 0 2 0 -1 2
s_2 0 -5 0 -2 1 0 1
z 0 -1 1 -3 0 2 1
Z 0 3 0 1 0 1 13

No negative entry remains. Optimal: x = 2, y = 0, z = 1, s_2 = 1, Z = 13. Product B is not made.

Check machine 4 + 0 + 1 = 5 \le 5 (used up), labour 8 + 0 + 2 = 10 \le 11 (slack s_2 = 1), material 6 + 0 + 2 = 8 \le 8 (used up).

The shadow prices under s_1, s_2, s_3 are 1, 0, 1: an extra machine hour is worth Rs 1,000, an extra labour hour is worth nothing (there is already a spare hour), an extra kg of material is worth Rs 1,000.

The entry 3 under y is the reduced cost: forcing one unit of B into the plan would lower profit by 3.

Reading special cases from the tableau

What each special case looks like in a simplex tableau
  • Unbounded: the entering column has no positive entry, so no ratio can be formed and the variable can grow forever.
  • Alternative optima: in the final tableau a non-basic variable has a 0 in the objective row. Pivoting on it gives another optimal corner with the same Z.
  • Degenerate: two rows tie in the minimum-ratio test. After the pivot one basic variable equals 0.
  • Infeasible (with \ge constraints): an artificial variable stays positive in the final tableau (big-M, below).
Worked example: a degenerate corner

Maximise Z = x + y subject to x \le 2, y \le 2, x + y \le 4. All three lines pass through (2, 2).

Basis x y s_1 s_2 s_3 RHS
x 1 0 1 0 0 2
s_2 0 1 0 1 0 2
s_3 0 1 -1 0 1 2
Z 0 -1 1 0 0 2

y enters, and the ratios for s_2 and s_3 are both 2/1 = 2 (a tie). Choosing s_2 gives x = 2, y = 2 and s_3 = 0, Z = 4. The slack s_3 is still basic but equals zero: the corner (2, 2) is degenerate.

The solution is correct; the only risk is that a pivot with a zero ratio may not improve Z, and in rare cases the method can cycle. Practical codes use tie-breaking rules (for example Bland's rule: choose the lowest-numbered candidate).

Sensitivity analysis: how long does the answer stay valid?

Prices and resource limits change. We can read how far, without re-solving, from the final tableau of the product-mix problem (maximise 3 x + 2 y, testing x + y \le 4, soldering x + 3 y \le 6).

Worked example: ranging the right-hand side and a profit

Testing hours b_1. The final basis is \{x, s_2\} with x = b_1 and s_2 = 6 - b_1. Both must stay \ge 0, so 0 \le b_1 \le 6. Within that range the shadow price 3 holds: b_1 = 4 \to Z = 12, b_1 = 5 \to Z = 15, b_1 = 6 \to Z = 18.

Beyond 6 hours, soldering (x \le 6 when y = 0) becomes the limit and extra testing time is worthless. Profit of a router kit c_1 (currently 3).

The corner A(4, 0) stays optimal while 4 c_1 \ge 3 c_1 + 2 (compare with B(3, 1)), that is c_1 \ge 2. At c_1 = 2 the corners A and B tie at Z = 8 (multiple optima); at c_1 = 1.5 the best plan jumps to B with Z = 6.5.

The big-M method (artificial variables)

A \ge or = constraint has no slack variable that can start the basis. We add an artificial variable a_i \ge 0 and charge it a huge penalty M in the objective (-M a_i when maximising, +M a_i when minimising).

The simplex method then drives the artificial variables to zero if the problem is feasible. If an artificial variable is still positive at the optimum, the original problem is infeasible.

The two-phase method does the same in two stages. Minimisation problems can also be solved through the dual (next section), which avoids artificial variables.

6.3 Duality

Every LPP (the primal) has a companion LPP (the dual). For the primal maximise c^{T} x subject to A x \le b,\ x \ge 0, the dual is minimise b^{T} w subject to A^{T} w \ge c,\ w \ge 0.

Rules: the number of dual variables equals the number of primal constraints; the RHS of the primal becomes the objective of the dual; the objective coefficients become the RHS; the inequality direction reverses; the matrix is transposed.

Worked example: writing and solving the dual

Primal: maximise Z = 3 x + 2 y s.t. x + y \le 4, x + 3 y \le 6. Dual: minimise W = 4 u + 6 v s.t. u + v \ge 3 (from x), u + 3 v \ge 2 (from y), u, v \ge 0.

Corner points of the dual region: (3, 0) (where u + v = 3 meets v = 0) with W = 12; (0, 3) with W = 18 and the point where the two lines meet, u + v = 3, u + 3 v = 2: v = -0.5, not allowed. The minimum is W = 12 at u = 3, v = 0.

It equals the primal maximum 12, and u = 3, v = 0 are the shadow prices read from the simplex tableau.

Duality theorem. If the primal has an optimal solution, so has the dual, and the optimal values are equal. Weak duality: any feasible Z \le any feasible W.

Why it matters: the dual often has fewer constraints (easier to solve), and its variables are the economic value of each resource.

Solving a minimisation problem through its dual

A minimisation problem with \ge constraints cannot start the simplex method directly (there is no slack to form a starting corner). Its dual is a maximisation with \le constraints, which can.

Rule: for minimise c^{T} x subject to A x \ge b, x \ge 0 the dual is maximise b^{T} w subject to A^{T} w \le c, w \ge 0.

Worked example: the hostel diet by simplex on the dual

Primal: minimise Z = 20 x + 30 y s.t. 2 x + y \ge 8, x + 2 y \ge 10. Dual: maximise W = 8 u + 10 v s.t. 2 u + v \le 20 (from the column of x), u + 2 v \le 30 (from the column of y), u, v \ge 0.

Basis u v s_1 s_2 RHS ratio
s_1 2 1 1 0 20 20
s_2 1 2 0 1 30 15
W -8 -10 0 0 0

v enters (most negative -10), s_2 leaves (ratio 15). After pivoting:

Basis u v s_1 s_2 RHS ratio
s_1 3/2 0 1 -1/2 5 10/3
v 1/2 1 0 1/2 15 30
W -3 0 0 5 150

u enters, s_1 leaves (pivot \frac{3}{2}):

Basis u v s_1 s_2 RHS
u 1 0 2/3 -1/3 10/3
v 0 1 -1/3 2/3 40/3
W 0 0 2 4 160

Optimal dual: u = \frac{10}{3}, v = \frac{40}{3}, W = 160. The minimum diet cost is Rs 160, equal to W by the duality theorem.

Reading the primal answer: the entries of the objective row under the slack variables s_1, s_2 are the primal variables: x = 2, y = 4. This matches the corner found graphically.

Complementary slackness and what the dual variables mean

At the optimum, a constraint and its partner variable are never both loose: if a constraint has slack, its dual variable is 0; if a dual variable is positive, its constraint is tight.

Check with the diet u = \frac{10}{3} > 0 and v = \frac{40}{3} > 0, and indeed both nutrient constraints are exactly met (2 \cdot 2 + 4 = 8 and 2 + 2 \cdot 4 = 10). In the product-mix problem, soldering has 2 spare hours and its shadow price is 0.

Interpreting dual variables

A dual variable is the marginal value of one more unit of its resource.

In the diet, u = \frac{10}{3} says that one extra unit of protein requirement raises the cheapest cost by about Rs 3.33, and v = \frac{40}{3} says one extra unit of iron raises it by about Rs 13.33.

A manager can use these numbers to decide what is worth buying more of: pay up to the shadow price for another unit of a scarce resource, never more.

Four possible outcomes for a primal-dual pair

(1) both have optimal solutions with equal values; (2) the primal is unbounded and the dual is infeasible; (3) the dual is unbounded and the primal is infeasible; (4) both are infeasible. It is impossible for one to have an optimum and the other not.

6.4 Solving linear systems on a computer

Matrix inversion method

Write the system as A X = B. If \det A \ne 0 then X = A^{-1} B, where A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det A}\,\mathrm{adj}\,A.

Worked example: matrix inversion

Solve 2 x + y = 5, x + 3 y = 10. Here A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \det A = 6 - 1 = 5, A^{-1} = \frac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.

Then X = \frac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \cdot 5 - 10 \\ -5 + 2 \cdot 10 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.

Check 2 + 3 = 5 and 1 + 9 = 10.

Inversion is clear on paper but costs about n^{3} operations and is less accurate than elimination, so software solves A X = B directly without forming A^{-1}.

Gauss elimination

Use row operations to turn the augmented matrix [A \mid B] into upper-triangular form (forward elimination), then solve from the last equation upward (back substitution).

Partial pivoting swaps rows so that the pivot is the largest available entry in its column, which controls rounding error.

Worked example: Gauss elimination

Solve 2 x + y - z = 8, -3 x - y + 2 z = -11, -2 x + y + 2 z = -3.

Augmented: \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 2 & 1 & -1 & 8 \\ -3 & -1 & 2 & -11 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -3 \end{array}\right]. R_{2} \leftarrow R_{2} + \frac{3}{2} R_{1}: (0,\ 0.5,\ 0.5 \mid 1). R_{3} \leftarrow R_{3} + R_{1}: (0,\ 2,\ 1 \mid 5). R_{3} \leftarrow R_{3} - 4 R_{2}: (0,\ 0,\ -1 \mid 1).

Back substitution: -z = 1 \Rightarrow z = -1; 0.5 y + 0.5(-1) = 1 \Rightarrow y = 3; 2 x + 3 + 1 = 8 \Rightarrow x = 2. Solution (2, 3, -1). Check in the second equation: -6 - 3 - 2 = -11.

Work for a system of n equations is about \frac{2}{3} n^{3} multiplications. If a zero pivot cannot be removed by swapping rows, \det A = 0 and the system has no unique solution.

Gauss-Seidel iteration

For large sparse systems an iterative method is better: start with a guess and improve it. Solve the i-th equation for x_{i} and use every new value immediately.

Convergence is guaranteed when the matrix is strictly diagonally dominant (|a_{ii}| > \sum_{j \ne i} |a_{ij}| in each row); arrange the equations that way first.

Worked example: Gauss-Seidel

Solve 10 x + y + z = 12, 2 x + 10 y + z = 13, 2 x + 2 y + 10 z = 14 (diagonally dominant). Formulas: x = \frac{12 - y - z}{10}, y = \frac{13 - 2 x - z}{10}, z = \frac{14 - 2 x - 2 y}{10}. Start (0, 0, 0).

Iteration x y z
1 1.2000 1.0600 0.9480
2 0.9992 1.0054 0.9991
3 0.9996 1.0002 1.0001
4 1.0000 1.0000 1.0000

The solution is (1, 1, 1). Iteration 1: x = (12 - 0 - 0)/10 = 1.2; y = (13 - 2.4 - 0)/10 = 1.06 (it uses the new x); z = (14 - 2.4 - 2.12)/10 = 0.948. Stop when two successive iterations differ by less than the tolerance.

Gauss-Jordan elimination and the inverse by row operations

Gauss-Jordan continues elimination until the left block becomes the identity. Applied to the augmented matrix [A \mid I], it turns I into A^{-1}.

This is how a computer (or Excel's MINVERSE) gets an inverse, and it avoids the long adjoint calculation for 3 \times 3 and larger matrices.

Worked example: inverse of a 3 by 3 matrix

Find A^{-1} for A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} and solve 2 x + y + z = 7, x + 3 y + 2 z = 13, x = 1. Start with [A \mid I] and use row operations (a row swap is always allowed).

  1. R_{1} \leftrightarrow R_{3}: rows become (1, 0, 0 \mid 0, 0, 1), (1, 3, 2 \mid 0, 1, 0), (2, 1, 1 \mid 1, 0, 0).
  2. R_{2} \leftarrow R_{2} - R_{1} gives (0, 3, 2 \mid 0, 1, -1); R_{3} \leftarrow R_{3} - 2 R_{1} gives (0, 1, 1 \mid 1, 0, -2).
  3. R_{2} \leftrightarrow R_{3}, so the pivot of column 2 is 1: rows (0, 1, 1 \mid 1, 0, -2) and (0, 3, 2 \mid 0, 1, -1).
  4. R_{3} \leftarrow R_{3} - 3 R_{2}: (0, 0, -1 \mid -3, 1, 5); then R_{3} \leftarrow -R_{3}: (0, 0, 1 \mid 3, -1, -5).
  5. R_{2} \leftarrow R_{2} - R_{3}: (0, 1, 0 \mid -2, 1, 3).

A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & -1 & -5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \det A = -1.

Then X = A^{-1} B with B = (7, 13, 1)^{T}: x = 1, y = -14 + 13 + 3 = 2, z = 21 - 13 - 5 = 3. Solution (1, 2, 3). Check: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 and 1 + 6 + 6 = 13.

If any column has no non-zero pivot available, \det A = 0 and no inverse exists; the system then has either no solution or infinitely many.

Why pivoting matters

Computers keep only a few significant digits, so dividing by a tiny pivot magnifies rounding errors. Take 0.0001 x + y = 1, x + y = 2, whose true solution is x = 1.0001, y = 0.9999, and imagine a machine that keeps 3 significant figures.

Worked example: elimination with and without pivoting

Without pivoting. The multiplier is 1 / 0.0001 = 10^{4}. Row 2 becomes (1 - 10^{4} \cdot 0.0001) x + (1 - 10^{4}) y = 2 - 10^{4}, i.e. -9999 y = -9998. Rounded to 3 figures, this is -10000 y = -10000, so y = 1.00.

Back substitution gives x = (1 - y) / 0.0001 = \mathbf{0}. The answer x = 0 is badly wrong. With partial pivoting. Swap the rows so that the larger entry 1 is the pivot: x + y = 2 and 0.0001 x + y = 1.

The multiplier is 0.0001: (1 - 0.0001) y = 1 - 0.0002, which rounds to 1.00 y = 1.00, y = 1.00 and x = 2 - 1 = \mathbf{1.00}. Correct to the 3 figures kept.

Rule for hand and machine work

At each step, choose as pivot the entry of largest absolute value in the column (among the remaining rows) and swap it into place. It costs only a comparison and a row swap, and it keeps every multiplier at most 1 in size.

Ill-conditioned systems

Some systems are ill-conditioned: tiny changes in the data change the answer enormously, whatever the method. Consider x + y = 2 and x + 1.0001 y = 2.0001. Its solution is (1, 1).

Change the right-hand side by only 0.0001 to 2.0002 and the solution jumps to (0, 2). The two lines are almost parallel, so their intersection slides a long way when one line moves slightly.

The condition number \kappa (A) = \|A\| \, \|A^{-1}\| measures this magnification; here \kappa \approx 40{,}000. A well-conditioned matrix has \kappa near 1.

With \kappa \approx 10^{k} you lose about k decimal digits of accuracy, so one should check the residual B - A X and, if possible, rescale or reformulate the problem.

LU factorisation: elimination you can reuse

Gauss elimination can be recorded as a product A = L U, where U is the upper-triangular matrix produced by forward elimination and L is a lower-triangular matrix holding the multipliers (1 on the diagonal).

Once A = L U is known, any new right-hand side B is solved cheaply in two triangular steps: L Y = B (forward substitution) then U X = Y (back substitution). Only the factorisation costs \frac{2}{3} n^{3}; each new B costs about n^{2}.

Worked example: LU for the earlier system

For A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ -3 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} the multipliers used in the Gauss elimination example were l_{21} = -\frac{3}{2}, l_{31} = -1, l_{32} = 4, giving

L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{3}{2} & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad U = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}.

Check, row 3 of L U: -1 (2, 1, -1) + 4 (0, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}) + (0, 0, -1) = (-2, 1, 2), which is row 3 of A. Now solve for a new right-hand side B = (1, 0, 3)^{T} without repeating elimination.

Forward: y_{1} = 1; -\frac{3}{2} y_{1} + y_{2} = 0 \Rightarrow y_{2} = 1.5; -y_{1} + 4 y_{2} + y_{3} = 3 \Rightarrow y_{3} = -2.

Back: -z = -2 \Rightarrow z = 2; \frac{1}{2} y + \frac{1}{2} (2) = 1.5 \Rightarrow y = 1; 2 x + 1 - 2 = 1 \Rightarrow x = 1. Solution (1, 1, 2).

Jacobi against Gauss-Seidel, and the need for diagonal dominance

The Jacobi method is the simpler cousin of Gauss-Seidel: every new value is computed from the old iteration only. Gauss-Seidel uses new values as soon as they exist, so it normally converges about twice as fast.

Both need a (nearly) diagonally dominant matrix and the equations written in the right order.

6.5 Solving non-linear equations f(x) = 0

Bisection method

If f is continuous on [a, b] and f(a) f(b) < 0, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a root in between. Take the midpoint m = \frac{a + b}{2}; keep the half where the sign changes; repeat.

After n steps the interval has length \frac{b - a}{2^{n}}, so the iterations needed for tolerance \varepsilon are n \ge \log_{2} \frac{b - a}{\varepsilon}. It always converges, but slowly (one binary digit per step).

Worked example: bisection for x^{3} - x - 2 = 0

f(1) = -2 < 0 and f(2) = 4 > 0, so a root lies in [1, 2].

n a b m f(m)
1 1 2 1.5 -0.1250
2 1.5 2 1.75 1.6094
3 1.5 1.75 1.625 0.6660
4 1.5 1.625 1.5625 0.2522
5 1.5 1.5625 1.53125 0.0591
6 1.5 1.53125 1.5156 -0.0341
7 1.5156 1.53125 1.5234 0.0123

After 7 steps the root is in [1.5156, 1.5313], about 1.52. Accuracy 0.001 needs n \ge \log_{2} (1 / 0.001) = 9.97, so 10 iterations.

Newton-Raphson method

Replace the curve by its tangent at the current guess and take the tangent's zero as the next guess:

x_{n+1} = x_{n} - \frac{f(x_{n})}{f'(x_{n})}.

Near a simple root it converges quadratically (the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step), but it needs f', can fail if f'(x_{n}) \approx 0, and may diverge from a bad start.

Worked example: Newton-Raphson for the same equation

f(x) = x^{3} - x - 2, f'(x) = 3 x^{2} - 1, x_{0} = 1.5. x_{1} = 1.5 - \frac{-0.125}{5.75} = 1.521739. x_{2} = 1.521739 - \frac{f(1.521739)}{f'(1.521739)} = 1.521380. The next step stays at 1.52138.

Root \approx 1.52138 in two steps, against ten bisection steps for a similar accuracy.

Choosing a method. Use bisection when a safe bracket exists and reliability matters; Newton-Raphson when f' is easy and a good start is known; in practice, software starts with bisection and switches to Newton-like steps.

Finding a starting bracket

Both methods need a good start. Tabulate f at integers and look for a sign change. For f (x) = x^{3} - x - 2: f (0) = -2, f (1) = -2, f (2) = 4.

The sign changes between 1 and 2, so a root lies in [1, 2]; since f' (x) = 3 x^{2} - 1 > 0 for x \ge 1 the function is increasing there and the root is unique.

Plotting f (or using a spreadsheet column of values) is the quickest way to bracket roots of other equations.

Regula falsi (false position)

Bisection ignores the sizes of f (a) and f (b). Regula falsi joins (a, f (a)) and (b, f (b)) by a straight line and takes the point where it crosses the x-axis:

c = \frac{a f (b) - b f (a)}{f (b) - f (a)}.

Then it keeps the sub-interval where the sign still changes, exactly like bisection.

Worked example: regula falsi for x^{3} - x - 2 = 0 on [1, 2]

f (1) = -2, f (2) = 4. c_{1} = \frac{1 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot (-2)}{4 - (-2)} = \frac{8}{6} = 1.33333, f (c_{1}) = -0.96296 < 0, so a = 1.33333.

Step c f (c) End kept
1 1.33333 -0.96296 a \leftarrow c
2 1.46269 -0.33334 a \leftarrow c
3 1.50402 -0.10182 a \leftarrow c
4 1.51633 -0.02989 a \leftarrow c
5 1.51992 -0.00868 a \leftarrow c

The estimates approach 1.52138 steadily and the error shrinks by a roughly constant factor (about 3.4) each step: linear convergence, but faster than bisection.

Notice that the end b = 2 never moves; for a curve bent like this the method stays "stuck" on one side, which is its known weakness.

Secant method

The secant method takes the same chord idea but drops the bracketing requirement and always uses the two most recent points: x_{n+1} = x_{n} - \dfrac{f (x_{n}) (x_{n} - x_{n-1})}{f (x_{n}) - f (x_{n-1})}.

It needs no derivative (unlike Newton-Raphson) and converges faster than regula falsi, with order about 1.618, but it can leave the interval and is not guaranteed to converge.

Worked example: secant for the same equation, x_{0} = 1, x_{1} = 2

x_{2} = 1.33333 (f = -0.96296); x_{3} = 1.46269 (f = -0.33334); x_{4} = 1.53117 (f = 0.05863); x_{5} = 1.52093 (f = -0.00269); x_{6} = 1.52138 (f = -0.00002). Five steps give 1.52138 to five decimals, with no derivative needed.

Speed of convergence compared

If e_{n} is the error after n steps, a method has order p when e_{n+1} \approx C\, e_{n}^{p}. Bisection and regula falsi are order 1 (linear); the secant method is order \approx 1.62; Newton-Raphson is order 2 (quadratic).

In decimal digits: bisection gains 0.3 digit per step, Newton roughly doubles the digits.

Method Order Needs f'? Needs a bracket? Always converges?
Bisection 1 No Yes Yes
Regula falsi 1 No Yes Yes
Secant 1.62 No No No
Newton-Raphson 2 Yes No No

When Newton-Raphson fails

The tangent idea can go wrong. Typical failures: (1) f' (x_{n}) = 0 (flat tangent): division by zero or a gigantic jump.

(2) A cycle: for f (x) = x^{3} - 2 x + 2 with x_{0} = 0, the tangent at 0 hits the axis at 1, and the tangent at 1 hits the axis at 0, so the iterates are 1, 0, 1, 0, \dots forever although a real root exists near -1.77.

(3) Divergence: for f (x) = \sqrt[3]{x} the root is 0, but x_{n+1} = -2 x_{n}, so every step doubles the distance. (4) A different root than the one wanted when the start is far away.

Safeguards in practice

Plot or tabulate first; start Newton-Raphson inside a bracket; stop and switch to bisection if a step leaves the bracket or if |f' (x_{n})| is tiny; limit the number of iterations (for example 50); and test the answer by checking |f (x_{n})| as well as |x_{n+1} - x_{n}|.

Newton-Raphson as a square-root algorithm

For f (x) = x^{2} - a the formula becomes x_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( x_{n} + \dfrac{a}{x_{n}} \right), the ancient Babylonian method, which calculators and sqrt routines still use in some form: each new guess is the average of x_{n} and a / x_{n}.

Worked example: \sqrt{10}

Start with x_{0} = 3. x_{1} = \frac{1}{2} (3 + \frac{10}{3}) = 3.1666667; x_{2} = \frac{1}{2} (3.1666667 + \frac{10}{3.1666667}) = 3.1622807; x_{3} = 3.1622777; x_{4} = 3.1622777.

The digits that are correct go 1 \to 3 \to 6 \to 8+, roughly doubling each step, as quadratic convergence promises.

Stopping criteria

An iteration must know when to stop.

Use one or more of: absolute change |x_{n+1} - x_{n}| < \varepsilon; relative change \frac{|x_{n+1} - x_{n}|}{|x_{n+1}|} < \varepsilon (better for very large or very small roots); residual |f (x_{n+1})| < \varepsilon; and a maximum number of iterations as a safety net.

A small residual does not guarantee a small error when f is very flat near the root, and a small change does not guarantee a small residual when f is very steep.

An application: the interest rate hidden in an EMI

A bank offers a loan of Rs 100,000 repaid in 12 monthly instalments (EMI) of Rs 9,000. What monthly interest rate r is it charging?

The present value of the instalments must equal the loan: 9000 \cdot \dfrac{1 - (1 + r)^{-12}}{r} = 100000. There is no formula that solves this for r, which is exactly the situation numerical methods are for.

Define h (r) = 9000 \cdot \dfrac{1 - (1 + r)^{-12}}{r} - 100000; h is positive when r is too small and negative when r is too large.

Worked example: bisection on [0.001, 0.05]

Try r = 0.001 (so h > 0) and r = 0.05 (so h < 0); the root is bracketed.

def bisection(f, a, b, tol=1e-6):
    n = 0
    while (b - a) / 2 > tol:
        m = (a + b) / 2
        if f(a) * f(m) < 0:
            b = m
        else:
            a = m
        n += 1
    return (a + b) / 2, n

def newton(f, df, x, tol=1e-10):
    n = 0
    while abs(f(x)) > tol:
        x = x - f(x) / df(x)
        n += 1
    return x, n

def gauss_seidel(A, b, tol=1e-6, max_iter=100):
    n = len(b)
    x = [0.0] * n
    for k in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        biggest = 0.0
        for i in range(n):
            s = sum(A[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(n) if j != i)
            new = (b[i] - s) / A[i][i]
            biggest = max(biggest, abs(new - x[i]))
            x[i] = new
        if biggest < tol:
            return x, k
    return x, max_iter

Formula and fact sheet

  • LPP: maximise Z = c^{T} x, A x \le b, x \ge 0. Optimum at a corner point.
  • Simplex: enter most negative objective entry; leave minimum ratio; pivot; stop when no negative entry remains.
  • Dual: \min b^{T} w, A^{T} w \ge c; optimal values are equal.
  • Gauss elimination: forward elimination then back substitution, about \frac{2}{3} n^{3} operations.
  • Gauss-Seidel: use new values at once; converges for strictly diagonally dominant A.
  • Bisection: n \ge \log_{2} \frac{b - a}{\varepsilon}. Newton-Raphson: x_{n+1} = x_{n} - \frac{f}{f'}.
  • Minimisation with \ge constraints: solve the dual (maximise b^{T} w, A^{T} w \le c); the primal answer is the objective-row entries under the slacks.
  • Special cases: no feasible region = infeasible; no positive entry in the entering column = unbounded; a zero in the objective row for a non-basic variable = multiple optima; a tied ratio = degenerate.
  • Shadow price of a resource = entry under its slack in the final objective row; it is valid while the basic variables stay \ge 0.
  • Partial pivoting: pick the largest |a_{ik}| in the column; LU: A = L U, then L Y = B and U X = Y; \kappa (A) = \|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|.
  • Regula falsi, order 1: the chord meets the axis at c = \left( a f (b) - b f(a) \right) / \left( f(b) - f (a) \right). Secant: order 1.62. Newton: order 2.
  • Babylonian square root: x_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( x_{n} + \dfrac{a}{x_{n}} \right).

Chapter summary

  • A linear programming problem has a linear objective and linear constraints; the optimum lies at a corner of the feasible region and can be found graphically (two variables) or by the simplex tableau.
  • The dual problem has the same optimal value, and its variables are the shadow prices of the resources.
  • Linear systems are solved by inversion, Gauss elimination or Gauss-Seidel iteration; roots of non-linear equations by bisection (safe, slow) or Newton-Raphson (fast, needs a derivative).
  • Real problems bring complications: infeasible, unbounded and multiple-optima LPPs, degenerate corners, minimisation through the dual, and sensitivity ranges for the shadow prices.
  • Numerical methods trade reliability for speed: pivoting and conditioning decide accuracy for linear systems, and the order of convergence (1, 1.62, 2) separates bisection, secant and Newton-Raphson. Newton-Raphson can cycle or diverge, so bracket first.
  • Excel (MINVERSE, MMULT, Solver, fill-down formulas), MATLAB (\, fzero, linprog) and Python (numpy, scipy) run all of these methods.
